title: Price the lockstep barrier in batched GPU physics from the solver's own iteration log
statement: On four MuJoCo Playground tasks (Go1 flat, Go1 rough terrain, Leap cube reorientation, humanoid) stepped at $W = 4096$ worlds in MJX and in MuJoCo Warp, log the engine's own per-world solver iteration count $N_{i,t}$ (world $i$, step $t$) with the iteration cap lifted so every world runs to its tolerance, for a random-init, a mid-training and a final checkpoint, and read off the realized barrier penalty $P = \mathbb{E}_t[\max_i N_{i,t}] / \mathbb{E}_{t,i}[N_{i,t}]$ and the censoring share $c_K = \Pr(N_{i,t} > K)$ at the shipped cap $K$. Fit the per-step time outside the solver $T_{\mathrm{fix}}$ (collision, kinematics, kernel launches) and the per-iteration batch time $\tau$ from a wall-clock sweep over forced iteration counts, and compute the Amdahl upper bound on what ideal iteration-level scheduling saves, $S = (T_{\mathrm{fix}} + \tau\,\mathbb{E}[\max_i N_i]) / (T_{\mathrm{fix}} + \tau\,\mathbb{E}[N])$. No re-stepping and no reference engine: every number is a profiler read of the training engine, and a secondary readout buckets worlds by their pre-solve contact count $n_{\mathrm{con},i}$ to see what share of the barrier a sort recovers without any asynchrony.
claim: In batched GPU physics the lockstep solve waits on the slowest world for a measurable share of step time: on at least one of four standard Playground tasks ideal iteration-level scheduling would cut step time by 30% or more, and the shipped iteration cap buys that speed by truncating the solve on more than 10% of world-steps.
trick: Read each world's solver iteration count from the engine's own counter; the slowest world's count over the average world's count is what the per-step barrier costs, and the share of worlds above the shipped cap is what the cap throws away.
why_now: MuJoCo Warp and NVIDIA Newton (2025) put a per-iteration batched Newton solve on the GPU, where lockstep across worlds is the kernel structure and not a choice; the card's paper (2610.29506, 2026-10) supplies a recipe for pricing a barrier from the asynchronous log alone, validated across 1.2x to 400x on CPU simulators (predicted-to-measured 0.84 to 1.19, median 0.996), and states (sec. 6.1) that closing a generation on the first finishers understates the barrier's cost, which is what an iteration cap does; MuJoCo Playground (2025) supplies standard tasks whose shipped caps are already low (C-W43-16: Go1 trains at K = 1). The checklist lesson of 2026-10-20 applies: the per-world trace is already logged (CPU mjData.solver_niter is documented; the batched counterpart is confirmed in step 0), so the 'why now' of the measurement is only that nobody has read it.

killing_experiment.design: Step 0 (half a day, no GPU): read the MJX and Warp solver source for the batched termination rule (early exit when all worlds meet tolerance, or a fixed count) and for the per-world iteration counter; if the batched engine lacks the counter, add an increment inside the existing per-iteration kernel (a ten-line patch; still a read, not a sweep). Step 1: 4 tasks x 3 checkpoints x 1000 steps x 4096 worlds in MJX with the cap lifted to 200 and tolerance at the engine default, logging $N_{i,t}$ and $n_{\mathrm{con},i,t}$; repeat in Warp for Go1 rough and Leap. Step 2: a timing sweep on one GPU (named in the record) with tolerance set to zero so every world runs exactly $K$ iterations, $K \in \{1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128\}$, three repeats, fitting step time $= T_{\mathrm{fix}} + \tau K$. Step 3: compute $P(W)$ for $W \in \{256, 1024, 4096, 16384\}$ by subsampling the logged batch (the paper's resampling recipe) and check against the realized per-step max at $W = 4096$; compute $S$, $c_K$ at each task's shipped cap, and the within-bucket penalty after sorting worlds by $n_{\mathrm{con}}$. Also record float32 as the dtype and the engine's tolerance floor before reading any count.
killing_experiment.kills_if: With the cap lifted, on all four tasks and all three checkpoints the Amdahl upper bound is $S < 1.15$ at $W = 4096$ (after step 0 confirms that the batched solve does run to the slowest world's count): iteration-level scheduling cannot pay even when its refill is free, and the lane's scheduler component is dropped. That negative is itself a recipe result that someone would cite: lifting the shipped cap to convergence costs under 15% of step time, so every Playground config should lift it. A second pre-registered kill is on the premise: if $c_K < 0.01$ at the shipped cap on the trained checkpoints, the cap is not binding there and 'caps trade physics for speed' is false for those tasks. Both outcomes are informative; a pass on $S$ is a budget for a scheduler, not a scheduler.

preregistered_surprise.expected: Because exact Newton converges by active-set identification (zero iterations when warm-started, iterations on constraint-set changes; checklist 2026-10-20), $N_{i,t}$ is a spike at 0 to 2 with a tail on worlds whose contact set just changed, so $P$ in iteration units lands between 3 and 20 at $W = 4096$ on every task (judgment probability 0.7), while the solver's share of lockstep step time $f = \tau\,\mathbb{E}[\max_i N_i] / (T_{\mathrm{fix}} + \tau\,\mathbb{E}[\max_i N_i])$ is between 0.3 and 0.7 on the contact-rich tasks (Leap, Go1 rough) and under 0.3 on Go1 flat; so $S$ reaches 1.3 or more on at least one task with probability 0.55 (judgment) and the kill ($S < 1.15$ everywhere) fires with probability 0.35. Censoring at the shipped cap: $c_K$ between 0.05 and 0.3 on the random-init checkpoint and lower on the trained one (probability 0.6). Secondary: sorting by $n_{\mathrm{con}}$ recovers less than half of the barrier (probability 0.6), because the tail is driven by contact-set changes, not by contact count.
preregistered_surprise.field_assumes: The lane's own origin text (themes.yaml L5: 'Iteration caps silently trade physics for speed') and CL-W43-01's first clause assume the cap buys speed; the card's paper states that closing on the first finishers understates the barrier's cost (sec. 6.1) and that the penalty is set by the spread (1.2x at runtime CV 0.05, 1.9x at CV 0.13 to 0.23, Tables 9 to 11); GPUSimBench (2607.13059, themes.yaml note) reports parallel scalability and batch non-determinism without a per-world solver spread. No engine we know of reports its per-world iteration distribution; the kill search quotes the MJX and Warp documentation on what the iteration setting is for.
preregistered_surprise.would_change: If $S \ge 1.3$ with $c_K > 0.1$: engine teams have a quantified Amdahl budget for an iteration-level or island-level scheduler, RL groups learn what fraction of their world-steps the cap cuts off, and the lane's scheduler component is funded with a number. If $S < 1.15$: in batched GPU mode the cap buys no speed worth having and should be lifted to convergence, a one-line change to every Playground config; the lane's premise is re-worded from 'caps trade physics for speed' to 'caps are inherited CPU-era defaults', and the scheduler is dropped. If the secondary readout shows sorting by $n_{\mathrm{con}}$ recovers most of $S$: the scheduler is a sort, not an asynchronous engine, and a colleague's Warp fork shrinks to a batching rule.

identifiability: $N_{i,t}$ is a deterministic function of the world's state, its warm start, the tolerance, the dtype (float32 in MJX and Warp; the acceptance floor near $8 \times 1.2 \times 10^{-7}$ relative from the 2026-10-20 checklist line is stated before any count is read) and the solver variant, so it is random only through the policy's action sampling, the domain-randomization draws and the reset states; it is a property of the (engine, task, policy, tolerance) tuple and not of the protocol, except through $W$, which enters as an order statistic and is reported as the curve $P(W)$ rather than one number. Worlds within a step are not independent draws (synchronized resets, one shared policy), so the realized per-step maximum over the batch actually run is the primary statistic and the i.i.d. resampling formula is only used to extrapolate across $W$. $T_{\mathrm{fix}}$ and $\tau$ are properties of the GPU and the engine build and are reported with both named. $S$ assumes a free refill of converged slots, so it is an upper bound: a kill on $S$ is one-sided and safe, and a pass on $S$ is a budget, not a measured speedup.
positioning_note: Solo: public engines, public tasks, under ten GPU-hours, no artifact needed; the result is a published number and a recipe line (lift the cap or build the scheduler). Lab-adjacent to engine builders (MuJoCo Warp / Newton, MJX), who can read the same counter from their own CI and have more reason to, and to the systems route as the consumer of the Amdahl budget. Not a frontier LLM lab's problem. The scheduler that a pass would fund is a lab or colleague piece (themes.yaml origin) and is not this probe. Lane L5 permits measuring and scheduling and forbids building engines; this measures.

scorecard.target_value: In print: themes.yaml L5 names iteration-level scheduling for batched Newton / conjugate-gradient solvers as the lane's systems lever and writes this measurement as its second kill test ('per-world solver-iteration distributions must be wide enough that iteration-level scheduling beats per-step sync by a margin the Amdahl model predicts'); the card's paper (2610.29506) validates the order-statistic barrier price across 1.2x to 400x and states that closing a generation on the first finishers understates the barrier's cost (sec. 6.1); GPUSimBench (2607.13059) measures scalability without a per-world solver spread. Who pays: engine teams deciding whether a world-asynchronous or island-level solver is worth building; every robotics RL group choosing the iteration cap in a Playground config; the lane itself, whose scheduler component lives or dies on this number.

impact_ceiling.middle: $S$ between 1.3 and 2 on the contact-rich tasks with a quantified censoring share at the shipped caps, agreeing across MJX and Warp: a workshop-length measurement that engine teams cite when setting cap defaults and that gives the lane's scheduler its Amdahl budget; requires the probe plus the Warp replication; probability 0.45 (judgment).

scorecard.kill_probe: Half a day of source reading, then 4 tasks x 3 checkpoints x 1000 steps x 4096 worlds with the cap lifted plus an eight-point timing sweep, about 8 GPU-hours (about $30), 4 days; kills if the Amdahl upper bound $S < 1.15$ on all four tasks at $W = 4096$; second kill on the premise if $c_K < 0.01$ at the shipped cap on trained checkpoints.
scorecard.density_and_ownership: From the card: all five neighbors are ABC / SMC (pyABC's generations 2203.13043; look-ahead scheduling 2305.00506 fills idle workers with next-generation work for 10 to 20%, up to 50%; anytime Monte Carlo 1612.03319 corrects length bias under a real-time budget; the particle cascade 1407.2864; Dynamic SBI 2510.13997); none measures a physics engine. From themes.yaml: GPUSimBench measures scalability and batch non-determinism without a per-world solver spread; GPUPhysBench grades code against expert code; Erez, Tassa and Todorov (ICRA 2015) is the CPU-era throughput-versus-accuracy comparison. Nobody we know of has published a per-world iteration distribution on standard GPU RL tasks; absence of a hit is not evidence. The kill search must search in the engine builders' words (island, load imbalance, warp divergence, early exit, convergence per environment, solver_niter, straggler world) across MJX / Warp / Newton / Genesis / PhysX docs, changelogs and issues; PhysX-style fixed-count PGS / TGS iterations have no convergence exit and so no barrier in this sense, which bounds the claim to Newton-type solvers with a tolerance. Kill search owed.
scorecard.why_now: MuJoCo Warp / Newton (2025) make the batched per-iteration GPU solve the shipped structure; 2610.29506 (2026-10) validates pricing a barrier from the log alone; Playground (2025) fixes the tasks and ships low caps. For the measurement itself the enabling piece is that the counter already exists, so the honest 'why now' is that nobody has read it (checklist 2026-10-20).
scorecard.register_and_not: Measurement in the systems register with a recipe consequence (lift or keep the cap; build or do not build the scheduler). Not a scheduler, not a new engine or contact model, not a fidelity audit, not an exploit test; it says nothing about whether the discarded physics matters to a policy, which belongs to the 2x2 return matrix and to C-W43-17.
